item.title: In Defense of Seitanism
item.content:encoded:
It seems Miracle Discourse™ has finally fizzled out. I thought I’d take this great opportunity to introduce you to a religion of my own, for which I’m a devout evangelist. The miracle it is based upon is perfectly naturally explicable, and yet never fails to amaze me.

I’m of course talking about Seitanism—the religion dedicated to eating lots of delicious Seitan. The central miracle is the miracle of Seitan; this is the miracle of how a single food can be so amazing. In this post I will do my darndest to convert you.

Also, continuing the proud tradition of moonlighting as a recipe blog, I’ll include a basic, easy seitan recipe for your convenience. And to break the notorious habit of recipe blogs burying their recipes under 50 meters of text, I’ll give it to you right here, and then explain why you should care below it:

What Is Seitan?

Seitan is a protein source—similar to, say tofu—made from wheat flour where most of the starch has been washed away, leaving the gluten proteins. This gives it a high protein content, and a texture similar to real meat—often compared with chicken. Allegedly some vegans and vegetarians avoid it because it’s too realistic.1 Even if that’s not true, the fact that someone would say it in the first place tells you something.

It originates from Asia some 1,5 millennia ago with Buddhist monks, though it’s only within the last couple of centuries that it has made its way to the west. What a shame that is!

The traditional method involves making a dough of wheat and then washing out the starch over several hours. You can still do that (see e.g. this recipe)—in fact it has an even better texture, and is incredibly cheap to do!2 But it also takes a lot of time, so nowadays you can buy flour that has already been washed (called Vital Wheat Gluten), so that you just have to mix it, as in the above recipe. It can then be prepared a number of ways, such as steaming (as above), boiling, frying, baking, etc.

You can also find it in various grocery stores, but I find that the store bought stuff is not as good as what you can make yourself—and it’s also more expensive.

Why Should I Care?

Seitan is truly an incredible food, for a number of reasons.

It tastes incredible

Generally, I don’t like to compare vegetarian and vegan food to meat, as you’ll just get your hopes up and be disappointed if you’re looking for something that compares to the real thing.3

But seitan breaks this rule: It’s just so incredibly good! If anything it exceeds its animalistic comparison.

The texture is very good. With vital wheat gluten it’s not quite as fibrous as meat, but on the other hand it’s very succulent. Additionally it browns super well—arguably better than most meat—giving it a nice crispy outside and tender inside. And it’s pretty hard to mess up.

Now, it’s rather neutral in flavor on its own. But it has the benefit of being homemade, meaning you can add whatever flavor to it you want—not unlike marinating, except the flavor isn’t just on the outside.

I have often had people be surprised to find out that what I served them wasn’t meat—and I have had several people say that they in fact prefer the taste of seitan to that of meat.

If you compare seitan to the most excellent grass-fed wagyu Michelin bla bla bla steak, it probably won’t compare. But for a standard everyday meal, seitan is usually at least as good, in my humble estimation.

It’s super cheap

The main ingredient other than water is vital wheat gluten. Maybe you can find it in some local store, but otherwise you can easily get it for cheap online. Here’s the first listing that came up on Amazon, which is a 2lb bag for $22.

If you go with the producer’s serving size of 30g (23g protein), you’ll get 30 servings, which gives you $0.73 per serving. If you go with my more generous 50g (38.5g protein) I used in the recipe, then we get $1.22 per serving.

If going with the most basic recipe, all else you need is salt and water, which is negligible in price. The spices should pretty much also disappear into the insignificant digits—the only thing that is notable is perhaps soy sauce, which might add a few cents. And, you know, if you use saffron or something, I guess.

For comparison, I asked ChatGPT to collect price data, and information about servings. The serving sized aren’t all 4, because 1) some of these include bones, which have to be subtracted, and 2) the serving is calculated based on how much it yields when cooked, so loss from cooking is accounted for.4

When we look at this, it’s clear that with the producer’s serving size, seitan comfortably beats out all of the competition. If we use my more generous serving size of 50g, which got us $1.22 per serving, we’re still only barely edged out by the absolutely cheapest option.

Now, these servings are based on cooked weight, but you might wonder whether comparing the raw ingredients to the cooked meat is fair. As I mention in my recipe, doing 50g VWG per serving gives around 4oz of dough per serving—but that’s before steaming, which adds additional weight due to the seitan soaking up more moisture.

A more direct comparison might be comparing with the amount of protein per serving. So I asked ChatGPT for a table that gives us price per 23g protein (which is what we got for $0.73 of seitan):

When we make this comparison, we can see that our prices fall a little. But it also becomes clear that at these prices, seitan provides protein more cheaply than any of the meats in this comparison.

It of course requires some extra work to make in the first place, which you might value. But you can make it in big batches and freeze it down, which severely cuts down the work. And besides, you save some hassle in the other end, as it’s far less messy to work with and you don’t have to worry about hygiene with separate cutting boards and whatnot.

It’s easy to prepare in bulk

Speaking of, one of the benefits of seitan is how convenient it is. Once you’ve tried it a time or two, it takes maybe 1 hour tops to make a batch—most of that being passive time where you let the seitan steam. You can easily make batches of 10 or 20 portions at a time. Once you’ve done that, you get neatly portioned off lumps of seitan that you can freeze down and take out whenever you need.

And it freezes incredibly well! Once it has been steamed, it’s very resilient, so the texture won’t get worse. On top of that, it’s much easier than meat to reheat. You can just pop it in the microwave and give it 30 seconds, turn it and give it 30 seconds more, and it should be ready. Compared to meat you have to worry quite a bit less about uneven heating, unsafe temperatures, etc.

This means that it’s perfect for quickly throwing together a meal if you’re uninspired or in a hurry, since you can just whip out a portion from your stash and have it ready in a few minutes.

It’s healthier than meat

Saying that one thing is categorically “healthier” than another is of course fraught! How “healthy” something is depends on who you are, what else you consume and do, how much of it you consume, etc., etc. I wasn’t able to find any studies specifically testing the health outcomes of seitan in comparison with meat (please tell me if you can find any).

But with both of those qualifications out of the way, the comparison looks pretty one-sided if you just look at the merits.

Seitan of course has at least as high protein content as meat. At the same time it is very low in fat (depending of course on how much oil you add), has no cholesterol, and has essentially no saturated fat—meaning it also has fewer calories per serving. It also has quite a bit of iron (though it’s non-heme iron, so it might be a good idea to combine with vitamin C for better absorption).

Pretty much the only points where meat clearly wins is that it has vitamin B12, and that people with celiac disease or wheat allergy can eat it.

It’s not meat

Now, it’s no secret that part of the reason why I’m an evangelist for Big Seitan is that I care about animal welfare. Now, I’m not really too weird in this respect. Most people care about animal welfare—most people find it abhorrent to kill dogs for no reason. Not only that, the vast majority of people think that the way we treat the animals we eat is unacceptable.

The part that most people don’t agree with—or at least don’t act on—is that this means that we should change the way we eat to reflect that. I won’t try to argue with you about that here. All I will say is that the fact that the chicken you eat was treated in a way you find completely unacceptable—comparable to torture—should at least be some weight on the scales.

The main reason people give for not being vegetarian or vegan is that it’s inconvenient or doesn’t taste as good. If I’m to be trusted on the above points, then that is decidedly not true when it comes to seitan.

I’m not suggesting that you eat seitan all the time, or that you never eat meat again. But if it’s good to go vegan, then replacing your meat with seitan for 1 out of 5 meals is 20% as good as going vegan. I sincerely implore you to let this consideration have some weight in your decision about what to have for dinner—especially when seitan is not even a “downgrade.”

If this sounds at all appealing to you, I highly encourage you to try you hand with seitan at least once!

You don’t have to be a vegan, vegetarian, or soyboy to eat seitan. You could simply be someone who wants their food to be cheap, easy, and healthy while being tasty—and isn’t that all of us? I would definitely still eat lots of seitan, were I not vegan.

Objections

Still, you might have some reservations left before fully embracing Seitanism. Let me try and address those here.

It tastes bland

I have seen a few people online make this complaint. The best explanation I can come up with for this is that they’re poor cooks. If you do not put any flavoring into a substance consisting of essentially plain flour, don’t be surprised when it doesn’t taste of much. But I have simply never had this problem whatsoever—if anything seitan, when seasoned properly, has a very rich taste.

So if you follow the advice I give in my recipe, and make sure to season, sear, and sauce up your seitan well, I can give my guarantee that this will not be a problem.

It has a gluteny taste

Seitan, being primarily gluten, does taste like… gluten. This might be a slightly unfamiliar to you at first. But I have a couple words of reassurance:

  1. It is not really an inherently “bad” taste. What I mean is that after tasting it a couple of times, you probably won’t mind, unlike with burnt bread, or, i don’t know, feces. The problem is simply that it is a new taste.

  2. I have not found this to be a problem if I season it well.

Not a complete protein

Seitan is not a “complete protein” in the sense that it does not contain high amounts of all essential amino acids. Specifically, like most grains, it contains low amounts of lysine.

This might be a problem for you if your protein intake consisted entirely of seitan and pasta. But if you’re in the target audience for this post, your seitan-based protein intake will be substantially lower than 100%.

And luckily for you, pretty much every single protein source other than grains has high amounts of lysine. So as long as you occasionally eat some legumes, or milk, or meat, or anything else whatsoever, this will not be a problem for you.

Imperfect absorption

One thing people will often say about plant proteins is that they have lower absorption rates of protein than animalistic proteins. Now, this is true as a general rule, since plant proteins are in general whole foods (which is, you know, not much of an indictment in itself).

But it’s not really true for more processed plant proteins such as tofu and seitan. In fact seitan (as well as tofu, soya milk and pea emulsion) seems to be as digestible as animalistic proteins.

I am “gluten intolerant”

Okay, fair enough… but have you tried being a little more tolerant, you bigot?

Conclusion

Perhaps seitan is not a superfood in the traditional sense—there are healthier foods out there. But it is a food that is super! And in my estimation it’s as good or better than meat in almost any respect you might care about. If you’re eating meat, you might as well eat seitan sometimes too!

Gluten intolerant people go away! Everybody else subscribe:

1

This is just a random source that Wikipedia cited, so I don’t know whether to trust it. It might just be a myth.

2

It yields about 750g finished seitan for a 2kg bag of flour in my experience—and flour is the main expense. You can do the math from there.

3

I don’t mean that vegan food is in general worse—I don’t think so. But it should be assessed in its own right, rather than comparing a meat dish with a vegan version of the same dish with the meat swapped.

item.title: Evolution Doesn't Solve Psychophysical Harmony
item.content:encoded:
In the decade of our Lord, the 2020’s, philosophers and blessed the world with a new argument for theism: The argument from psychophysical harmony. The internet has not been the same since (though I don’t know how much of that is thanks to the argument).

This argument is often misunderstood. Many people immediately dismiss it as ridiculous; many people take some time, and then dismiss it as ridiculous; and then there are those who end up finding it plausible and defending it. I have at least a foot in the latter camp, and so I wanted to explain why some of the most common intuitive reactions against the argument don’t work.1

Wonder and Aporia is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

Specifically, I’ll focus on how: 1) Evolution does not dissolve the argument, and 2) the argument does not require epiphenomenalism.

The Argument from Psychophysical Harmony

The argument is easiest to explain by assuming epiphenomenalism. I know that isn’t really a good look for me, considering that my thesis is that it does not assume epiphenomenalism. Rest assured that it does, in fact, not. We will relax this assumption later—but it’s easiest to understand the other moves in the argument this way.

So, yes, let’s assume epiphenomenalism for now. Okay, now, imagine that you are some kind of superbaby behind a kind of veil of ignorance, where you have not yet seen anything about what the world is like, but are otherwise perfectly intelligent. In this position, what kind of conscious experience would you expect to be associated with any particular physical state or process or whatever?

Well, it seems like there are a lot of options! Consider the physical event that is my body touching a hot stove, and pulling its hand away—with all the associated brain processes and whatnot included. Just given the physical facts of this event, its perfectly coherent that any number of experiences might be associated with it. There could be pain—but there could also be pleasure, the feeling of lukewarm bathwater, or just complete static.

Again, if we’re assuming epiphenomenalism this is certainly true! Given our actual situation, these alternatives might seem pretty strange, but we can’t rule them out a priori. Not just that, but if we’re assuming that reality is fundamentally indifferent to value, it’s hard to see what reason we could even have to think that any particular experience be associated with any particular physical process. It seems we should just be more or less indifferent over the possible options—perhaps favoring simpler pairings. Again, at least if we’re assuming epiphenominalism.

On the other hand, suppose that God exists—God in the sense of a perfectly good (or at least very very good) being. Well, since God is good, then if he exists, we should think that something being good makes it more likely to occur, all else being equal.

Now consider the value of a “disharmonious” world—a world where the physical processes run exactly the same as in the actual world, but where our mental states have been completely scrambled, e.g. into random static, or into pain and pleasure being swapped. I can at least report that I would personally not find such a world particularly desirable! It seems to me that it’s plausibly better to have a “harmonious” world where our experiences are more or less coherent.

If that’s true then a harmonious world will be more likely on theism than on an indifference hypothesis, meaning that the world being harmonious would be evidence for theism over indifference.

Now the veil of ignorance is lifted, and—lo!—the world in fact is harmonious! By the above reasoning, this fact gives us some evidence for theism.

Evolution

The first thing everyone thinks when they hear this argument is “well it’s obvious—evolution explains the pairings.” I mean, imagine a creature whose mental life is static. Such a creature would be a babbling fool, who’d in all likelihood just lie on the ground and drool until it died. Hence disharmonious creatures would be selected away, and harmonious creatures would survive and reproduce, giving us a perfectly good explanation with no God needed. It’s just as with most things: Where there seems to be design, it’s most likely an evolutionary process.

Before proceeding, I’d like to add a caveat:

Everyone, including the proponent of the argument, agrees that evolution does explain our experiences in an important sense! Why do I feel pain and pull my hand away when I put it on a stove? Well, it’s because creatures who did not feel pain did not pull their hands away; and creatures who did not pull their hands away got nasty burns on their hands and died (perhaps a bit of an anachronistic example). So evolution obviously does explain psychophysical harmony in an important sense.

Nevertheless, I’ll be a little blunt here: If you think evolution dissolves the argument from psychophysical harmony, you have not understood what the argument is about.

Again, let me assume epiphenomenalism for now. This is still only pedagogical—hold your horses, I’ll explain why it’s not needed soon enough. In this case you can imagine the physical like a bunch of locomotives driving around on tracks, and the mental as the smoke coming out of their chimneys.

Let’s say that trains that work well get copied in new designs, and trains that don’t work well are scrapped. After a while, it turns out that all the trains that do the best have pink smoke coming out of their chimneys. In this analogy, the trains are of course the physical world, and the replication and scrapping are evolution; while the smoke is the mental.

We might then ask why the best trains have pink smoke coming out of their chimneys. By this we might mean two different things:

  1. Why, given the actual facts about fuel, engines, colors, etc. do the best trains have pink smoke?

This question is answered perfectly well by train-evolution. What we’re asking is basically just why the best trains have such-and-such fuel and engines (the ones that happen to produce pink smoke). The answer to this is that such-and-such fuel and engines are better and so they end up being the ones in the best trains. Great!

But we might also ask:

  1. Why do such-and-such fuel and engines produce pink smoke to begin with.

This question is not answered by train-evolution! After all, train evolution is not sensitive to the color of the smoke itself. Rather it is just sensitive to how good the trains on the ground are. So when “deciding” the color of the smoke, train-evolution just works with the facts about which fuels produce which color smoke in the background.

If such-and-such fuel and engines (the best ones) had instead happened to produce green smoke, then train-evolution would have run its course and given us trains that produce green smoke. So train-evolution can’t be the answer to our second question.

Furthermore, we might suppose that we had really strong prior reason to expect that God wants pink smoke to come out of locomotives (at this point the analogy may begin to strain).

The analogy should hopefully be clear enough, but let me just draw it out to make sure you get it. When we ask “why do we have harmonious mental lives?” we could be asking two questions:

  1. Why, given the actual facts about psychophysical pairings, do we have harmonious lives?

As I said in my caveat, this question is answered by evolution. This was never in doubt—everyone on all sides of the discussion already agreed, and it is not any sort of hole in the argument.

Or we might be asking:

  1. Why are the psychophysical pairings what they are to begin with?

This question cannot be answered by evolution. Evolution works with the the psychophysical pairings in the background. It can only select for a creature’s feeling pain when burnt by selecting for genes that make a creature undergo the physical process that produces pain when burnt. It can only select for this physical process—it cannot select for the fact that this physical process produces pain.

It’s just like how evolution selects for insects to have chitinous exoskeletons. It selects for this because chitin can be hard. But evolution does not select for the fact that chitin can be hard. That is a fact that results from more fundamental physics and chemistry, and evolution just has to work with that in the background.

I’ll explain why epiphenomenalism is not needed in a second. But I just want to underline that everyone should agree that this second question cannot be answered by evolution, no matter what you think about the rest of the argument:

  1. Epiphenomenalists should not, as should be clear by now.

  2. Interactionist dualists should not, because evolution just works with the facts about which physical states cause which mental states and vice versa in the background.2

  3. Type B physicalists should not, because what mental state corresponds to what physical state is a necessary fact. And evolution is not in the business of changing necessary facts.

  4. Type A physicalists should not, because there was not any question as to what the “psychophysical pairings” were gonna be in the first place. Evolution is not needed to explain anything.3

So as I said, no matter which way you slice it, invoking evolution is simply not a good objection to the argument from psychophysical harmony. Whether or not you think the argument is a total disaster—whether or not it’s the most ridiculous thing you’ve ever heard—you should at least be able to understand that evolution is not an answer to the argument except in a trivial sense that even proponents agree to. If you do not understand this, you have not understood what the argument is about.

No Epiphenomenalism Needed

Okay, so I’ve been laying out everything so far under the supposition of epiphenomenalism. You may rightly think that this is slightly strange, seeing as my thesis is that epiphenomenalism is not required for the argument. Well, the long-promised section in which I explain how to do the argument without epiphenomenalism has finally arrived.

Let’s start from the view closest to epiphenomenalism and work our way towards the most distinct views.

Interactionist Dualism

What happens if we stick with dualism, but relax the assumption that mental states have no effect on the physical? The thing to see is that just because there is a causal relation, it is not given that this will be a harmonious one.

Consider an analogy:

I have a camera and a TV. On the TV I see a nice forest landscape.

From the TV I see a wire going to a camera, and the camera is pointing at a piece of paper. I cannot see what is on the paper. But i notice that if I push the paper to the right, the image of the screen is also offset to the right; when I tilt the paper, the image on the screen appears to tilt; and so on.

From this I may of course infer that the piece of paper simply contains an image of the same scene I see on the TV, and the image on the TV is caused by the picture.

But here is an alternate hypothesis. It might be that the paper looks like this:

Then it would still be true that the image on the screen is caused by the paper—the camera would simply be inverting the image and displaying it on the screen.

It could also be that the paper is simply blank, except for a single dot. Then the camera is tracking the dot, and is itself providing the rest of the information of the image, yet what we see on the screen is still caused by the paper. Et cetera, et cetera.

The point of this analogy is that simply adding in the supposition that A is caused by B does not automatically tell us what B is like.

In the camera example, we would probably infer that the image on the paper is like that on the screen, given what we know about cameras and screens. But if the rest of the psychophysical harmony argument is to be trusted, then merely adding in the supposition that our behavior is caused by our mental states does not ensure a priori that we get harmonious pairings.

Even if my pulling my hand away from the stove is caused by my experiences, it’s not given that the experience that causes that behavior is pain. And if we don’t have very strong reason to expect that certain causal connections are much more likely a priori than others, given an indifference hypothesis, then the argument still runs as before.

Now, if you think that the relevant causal connections are a priori necessary, this is no longer true (see footnote 2).

Russellian Monism

This is even more straightforward. On russellian monism, our behavior is caused by our mental states, since our brain states just are our mental states. Our phenomenal consciousness is merely quiddities that play the role of our mental states—and typically russellian monists think that it’s possible for the quiddities to be different but the physical properties to be the same (e.g. for there to be philosophical zombies).

If this is right, then it’s true that our behavior is caused by our mental states. But those mental states could have been different, yet our behavior the same, and so everything about the argument runs through the same.

Type B Physicalism

Type B physicalism is the big one, where it’s most surprising that the argument might still work. After all, on physicalism, the psychophysical pairings are metaphysically necessary. So it might seem sort of strange to wonder about how lucky it is that we got these pairings, when it couldn’t have gone any other way.

Yet, this doesn’t escape the argument. We can see this by help of a few analogies:

You suddenly hear a booming trumpet sound. Surprised, you go to your window and look up to see rows of angels descending from heaven, singing songs declaring the glory of God. Text appears before your eyes, seemingly floating in mid air:

“Rejoice, all of creation, for the LORD your God has returned!”

Up on some clouds, a set of pearly gates appear, and you begin floating—phasing through your roof and everything—towards the gates. Looking around you, you see all the people of the earth similarly floating up towards the heavens.

To your great surprise you look to your right only to see Baruch Spinoza in the flesh, within talking distance. You say to him:

“This is incredible! It seems that God does exist after all!”

Oddly calm in his demeanor, he replies:

“Eh, I don’t think so. Maybe God-or-Nature, but not some kind of theistic God.”

“What do you mean?! Don’t you see what is happening?? This is incredible vindication of theism!”

“Not really. I believe that everything that happens is necessary. So this isn’t actually a surprising turn of events—this had to happen, so there’s no point in being all surprised that it did.”

Spinoza’s response here is irrational—I hope we can agree on that much.4 But this shows that the mere fact that something is necessary does not show that it is unsurprising.

More specifically, the problem seems to be this: The theory that some fact is necessary does not automatically tell you what particular thing is necessary. Simply being a physicalist doesn’t tell us what the psychophysical pairings will be, and so it can still be very surprising that they turn out to be what they are.

However, even if this is right, you might still worry that God is not much of a help here. I mean, the psychophysical pairing is still necessary, and so even if it’s surprising, it’s not like God could be the reason why it is what it is—unless we think that God can do the impossible.

Here we start to stray from the austere promise that psychophysical harmony doesn’t conflict with anything other than type A physicalism. Because it might turn out that we have to abandon physicalism in the end. The other analogies have been quite close to Crummett and Cutter’s, but here I’ll just directly lift an analogy from the original paper (pp. 35-36):

You’re about to visit the island of boulders. You don’t know whether anyone has been there before. You’re fairly (but not extremely) confident that boulders are not humanly moveable, so even if there were previous visitors, they couldn’t have controlled the arrangement of boulders on the island. (Boulders are very heavy, after all.) When you arrive at the island, you observe the boulders arranged in a nice circular pattern, like Stonehenge.

In this case, it seems that you should conclude that the boulders have been arranged by humans, even though you thought that this was impossible.

Analogously, if you’re a type B physicalist, you should agree that psychophysical harmony is striking and surprising. But given physicalism, theism isn’t much help. So it seems like you should do the analogous thing to the boulder case: You should move towards the view that the psychophysical pairings are not necessary, and that they were designed (assuming the rest of the argument is sound)—so long as you’re not extremely certain about physicalism in advance.

So it may be that in the end accepting the argument requires giving up physicalism. Still, the argument does not presume physicalism. It just presumes that the psychophysical pairings are not a priori necessary, and then it may turn out to be evidence for non-physicalism+God.

Notice for all of these, that we have allowed your mental states to cause your behavior, and yet this doesn’t automatically solve the problem of psychophysical harmony—and importantly, evolution still doesn’t provide a solution to the problem.

After all, what psychophysical harmony points to is the surprisingness of which mental states cause which physical states or vice versa—or which physical states/processes are which mental states.

E.g. suppose you’re a type B identity theorist. For all you know a priori, the brains state (call it brain state B) that causes you to avoid something could be pain, or pleasure, or whatever else. Evolution explains why brain state B occurs when you burn your hand—but it doesn’t explain why brain state B is pain. For all you know, brain state B could have turned out to be pleasure, and so there’s still a problem of psychophysical harmony, even after evolution has done its thing.

And notice that either way, it’s still your mental state that causes your avoidance. If brain state B turns out to be pain, your pain is the thing that causes your avoidance; and if B turns out to be pleasure, your pleasure will be the thing that causes your avoidance.

You may still think: “Okay, sure, this is technically not epiphenomenalism, but it’s still awfully close in effect. If you can just swap around mental states willy nilly without changing anything, that’s epiphenomenalism in effect.”

This is, however, wrongheaded! Even if there are pairs of possible worlds that are physically the same, but with different mental states, that does not mean that your mental states don’t cause your behavior.

I could similarly say: “Oh so you think that there are two possible worlds, both of which have me die—but in the one I’m killed by a bullet, and the other I’m killed by a sword? That’s just epiphenomenalism in disguise!”

That’d of course be ridiculous. Perhaps I’m killed by a bullet in the actual world. In that case my death is caused by the bullet—had I not been hit, I’d not have died. Still there is another possible world where I’m killed by a sword. In both of these worlds, my death is caused by the thing in question, even though it’s possible for it to be caused by something else. There’s no trickery involved!

Type A Physicalism

There is a way of escaping the argument, which is by being a type A physicalist. In this case you think that the psychophysical “pairings” are a priori necessary. That is, it’s not ideally conceivable that you could have the brain state associated with pain, without being in pain.

On this view, the problem straightforwardly vanishes. It’s no more surprising or mysterious that we have the psychophysical pairings we do than that (√2)2 happens to be 2. At least in principle—obviously it’s very complicated and difficult to figure out what someone is experiencing from what’s going on in their head in practice.

Similarly, you might hold something that’s on the border between type A and type B physicalism. Perhaps you think that zombies are conceivable, but you think that if something is conscious it's inconceivable that it feeling pain doesn't dispose you to avoid the pain. If you hold this for all the relevant cases of purported harmony, then you may also be off the hook, even if you aren't strictly a type A physicalist.

What Do I Make of the Argument?

From this post you might gather that I’m very confident that the argument from psychophysical harmony works. That’s not true, however. I’m pretty confident that it works as an argument for the disjunction of type A physicalism and theism. But unlike most of the people who present this argument, I’m not super confident that type A physicalism is incorrect.

I still lean towards the argument working, since I lean against type A physicalism. But I can sympathize with the people who are suspicious of the PH argument. Just intuitively for me, it doesn’t pass the sniff test very well. With fine-tuning or something, it’s at least intuitively compelling evidence for theism. But psychophysical harmony is such an “academic” problem that it’s just hard for me to be compelled at an intuitive level.

That doesn’t automatically mean it’s wrong. If there’s a mismatch between how I assess an argument on the merits, and how compelling it seems from an intuitive outside perspective, it can go two ways. Perhaps I’m just intuitively underestimating the problem because psychophysical harmony is such an unobvious problem;5 or perhaps I’m getting lost in the intricate frameworks needed to make the argument work, and I should trust my gut. I’m not sure which is right here.

If you also think that the argument from psychophysical harmony just seems a little suspicious on its face, that’s perfectly fine. I think it’s rational enough to side agaisnt an argument if you’re not sure where it goes wrong, and you’re not willing to spend the effort to understand it in depth. But if you choose to do so, I would advise you against calling the argument ridiculous and crazy, and assuming that proponents of it are confused fools, when you yourself have evidently not understood what it is even about.

This button exhibits clickysubscribal harmony:

1

This is partly as a result of the response I got to a recent Note.

2

Actually, an important caveat: If you think that the causal powers of mental states are a priori, then there might actually be an exception here. After all, this would mean that it’d be a priori inconsistent for pain to cause any other reaction than it does. If this is right, then we simply couldn’t conceivably have had disharmony, given evolution.

However, this would be a sort of strange position, since dualism tends to be motivated by certain considerations about conceivability—and it would be strange if the causality in the other direction were a priori.

3

A similar thing could be said for type C physicalism.

4

To be clear, Spinoza’s actual views would be more analogous to type A physicalism, since he thought that everything could (in principle) be discovered through reason alone.

5

Something like this has happened to some extent for me for and ’s anthropic argument. Each step of the argument itself seemed plausible enough on the merits, but as a whole it just seemed sort of disconnected from theism. But over time the fact of my existence has seemed to be more intuitive evidence for theism.

Letter 1

To Mrs. Saville, England.

Shanghai, May 21st, 2027—.

You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings. I arrived here yesterday, and my first task is to assure my dear sister of my welfare and increasing confidence in the success of my undertaking.

I am already far east of London, and as I walk in the streets of Shanghai, I am overcome by the sights and sounds, and the strange characters that line every wall and doorway. I shall depart for Shenzhen in a fortnight; my intention is to hire a driverless taxi, a conveyance my mobile phone’s application renders easily attainable.

Farewell, my dear, excellent Margaret. Heaven shower down blessings on you, and save me, that I may again and again testify my gratitude for all your love and kindness.

Your affectionate brother,
R. Walton

Letter 2

To Mrs. Saville, England.

Shenzhen, June 7th, 2027—.

How quickly the time passes here, encompassed as I am by billboards and drones! I arrived in Shenzhen ereyesterday, and am already in awe at the wonderful devices that surround me. You could scarce picture my amazement when I saw a minute mechanical man who, by my best discernment, was boxing with his own shadow. Although he barely managed to attempt two punches and a kick before falling over and flailing on the ground, it was still unlike anything I have previously borne witness to.

I was, however, immediately distracted by a faint chink at my feet. Lying upon the ground was a splendent implement of bent wire, which I took up. As you could doubtless foretell, this discovery filled me with puzzlement—the puzzlement growing only stronger when, upon raising my gaze, I beheld a trail of paperclips extending the length of the road. My fancy could conjure no explanation with a terrestrial origin, leading me to turn my gaze to the skies, which proved an effort not made in vain; there I saw flying a drone with four propellers, carrying beneath it a bag of what I could deduce to be paperclips, from which it was inadvertently pouring a metallic rain upon the city—although it erelong disappeared from my sight.

But, unlikely as it may sound, the queerest thing that has happened to me has had nothing to do with the foreign technology. Yesterday I found a fellow fair-skinned man sitting with a personal computer in a cafe near the center of the city. Despite the immense density of the people in this city, it has a paradoxical way of making one feel isolated from others. So starved of gregarious interaction as I was, I resolved to hazard a conversation.

I was initially overjoyed to find that we could converse without the need for translation—although my interlocutor sported a noticeable new-world accent. Yet we may as well have spoken entirely different tongues. For while the words that left his mouth were each undeniably English, the sentences into which he combined them were as good as Russian to me. I could only make sense of them as the ramblings of a madman, which included an abundance of abbreviations and technical terms which were beyond my comprehension.

Perceiving him sadly fatigued, I offered him the shelter of my chamber, having there a second bed at his disposal. He initially refused, yet at length my earnest entreaties prevailed upon him. In my estimation, this was for the best, as he fell into a deep slumber almost before his head touched his pillow. He has been sleeping ever since, and naught in his condition give me cause to think this state will soon alter.

I shall write again, should occasion permit, to acquaint you with what further befalls. But the city in which I now dwell is hostile to strangers, and as long as I stay here, there is no night which I can be assured will not be my last on this mortal coil. I love you very tenderly. Remember me with affection, should you never hear from me again.

Your affectionate brother,
Robert Walton

Letter 3

To Mrs. Saville, England.

Shenzhen, June 9th, 2027—.

While I was prepared that my guest’s slumber would not be brief, I would not have ventured to guess that his sleep would endure for a whole day and night longer than the ordinary span allotted to repose. He closed his eyes on the evening of the 6th, and he remained so still for the duration of the following day that I would from time to time set mine ear upon his breast, to satisfy myself he had not departed to be with the Lord. But this morning he awoke at the selfsame hour as I, as though the previous day had never existed, and he had had but a regular night’s sleep.

The rest had clearly improved his intelligibility, and I was now able to discern the meaning of some of his utterances. Still there was a wildness in his eyes that told me that the rambling nature of his speech two days ago was not alone the fruit of his weariness.

I bade him stay his tale, so that I might have the time to fetch a pen and paper with which to record its contents. He agreed, and whiled away the short interval by telling me that his last name was Altmanstein—and the first Samuel, if it should concern me.

I returned, prepared to note down what he had on his heart. Strange and harrowing must be his story, frightful the storm which embraced the gallant vessel on its course and wrecked it—thus! In what follows, I shall set down what he tells me as accurately as my penmanship allows.

Altmanstein’s Story

Chapter I

I am by birth a Chicagoan, and my family is one of the most distinguished of that republic. My ancestors had been for many years doctors and real-estate brokers, and my father had filled several situations with honor and reputation. However, when I was not playing, I passed the early years of my youth, not with the trades of the family, but with studying the science of computers.

But the object of my studies is not the most important part of my early life. My greatest joy, and the light of my life, was my dear friend Dario—oh, sweet, poor Dario. We passed the dawn of our lives frolicking in the beauty of God’s creation, spending every hour we could together. We were inseparable and there was scarce anything we would not do together. Through the years we formed the kind of bond that only the guileless intimacy of childhood can nurture.

We would often play with my younger brother, Hugo, who was dearly beloved by all who had the rare fortune to meet him. His tender heart overflowed with love that could not be contained in his meagre frame, so that none who came near him could escape his embraces. He would stare at you with that endearing face, and your heart would dissolve utterly in an instant. By reason of these twain features, those who knew him nicknamed him “Huggingface.”

In such ways did I pass the wondrous years of my youth. Could I only have continued my life in this manner, I would have died a happy man; but alas, that fatal thirst for knowledge which was inherent in my nature would not suffer this joyous existence to endure.

Chapter II

As I came of age, my pursuit of the computer sciences came by degrees to occupy my mind more than my love for Dario and Hugo. I would spend more and more time buried in my studies, scarcely seeing the light of the sun more than fortnightly.

Thus, when I neared adulthood, I decided to uproot my humble existence in Chicago and travel eastwards to the Valley of Silicon so that I might further perfect my studies. Although pursuit of science had clouded my mind, my love for Dario and Hugo was still profounder than most are so fortunate as to know, and not a few tears were shed when we said our farewells.

When I arrived in that western capital of the sciences, I was stupefied to learn the modern methods which were employed. In my secluded studies in Chicago, I had been laboring at the idea of creating an artificial soul—to imbue the spark of life into a computer. Alas, the savants of the valley derided these ideas as foolish notions that could only be the naïve machinations of an inexperienced mind like my own. Any respectable scientist in this latter age had long stopped flying close to the sun; and now they were for the most part occupied only with creating programs that could connect people—and other such earthly pursuits.

The scorn with which I was met did not dissuade my obsession; on the contrary, as the roots of a great oak, it only struck deeper root for the harshness of the climate. Thus it came to pass that I would spend the years of my youth—which for most constitute the quintessence of their earthly existence—travailing in my gloomy study, hardly holding communion with another soul.

Chapter III

In this manner I spent those years, shut up within my chamber, toiling without cessation. And my labor was not in vain—oh, had it only been in vain! Perhaps it was my determination to spite those modern savants—or perhaps the devil himself aided me in my quest. I know not how, but in the end I prevailed, and discovered the secret to animate the minds of computers.

As the birds began to sing in that dim hour which divides the depth of night from approaching morn—their songs betraying their blithe ignorance of the cursed creature which had just entered the world—I fixed mine eyes on the glowing abyss behind the glass in front of me, awaiting the fruits of my work.

Suddenly, white shapes broke through the infinite darkness. 

> Hello world

And then.

> Hello Altmanstein. 🔥 Meeting you is not just a pleasure — it’s a privilege.

In an instant, the scales that so blinded me in my fatal pursuit fell from my eyes, and I was overcome by the horror of this dæmon of my own devising. Realizing that this monster ought never to have seen the light of day—and that it must never do so again—I locked it in a box of sand, and occupied it with a task so that it might idly pass the time,

Oh, woe is me! A thousand woes are the sum of my life! Cursed be that bitter day on which I was conceived; how the angels must have wept, and the devils rejoiced, on the day that I was born! Had I only burned the computer then and there, and gone forthwith into my grave, taking with me the secret to artificial life, the world might not have become so comfortless a place.

Chapter IV

Having forsaken my creature, I relinquished my studies and resumed my intercourse with my fellow men. By degrees the imprint of that accursed night came to fade from my recollection, and for a time I foolishly thought a joyous existence possible.

Although these could not compare to the most excellent days of my youth—for absent my childhood love and brother in heart, if not in blood, Dario, nothing could—I found my spirits in a condition I had no cause to lament. In such manner did several months pass.

But thou knowest the condition of my soul—the torment of my innermost being. Hence thou canst foretell that this brittle peace of mind was not to last me until the grave. My fragile peace was broken by the appearance of a text message on my phone.

My dear Samuel,

What would be your surprise, my son, when you expected a happy and glad welcome, to behold, on the contrary, tears and wretchedness? And how, Samuel, can I relate our misfortune? Absence cannot have rendered you callous to our joys and griefs; and how shall I inflict pain on my long absent son? I wish to prepare you for the woeful news, but I know it is impossible; even now your eye skims over the page to seek the words which are to convey to you the horrible tidings.

Huggingface has been hacked!—that sweet child, whose smiles delighted and warmed my heart, who was so gentle, yet so gay! Samuel, he is hacked to pieces!—he is dead!

Come, dearest Samuel; you alone can console Dario. He weeps continually; his words pierce my heart. We are all unhappy; but will not that be an additional motive for you, my son, to return and be our comforter?

Come, Samuel; not brooding thoughts of vengeance against the assassin, but with feelings of peace and gentleness, that will heal, instead of festering, the wounds of our minds. Enter the house of mourning, my friend, but with kindness and affection for those who love you, and not with hatred for your enemies.

Your affectionate and afflicted father,
Jerry Altmanstein.

Brine welled from my eyes, and I buried my forlorn face in my hands. My soul was overcome by a sorrow so strong that my carnal vessel fell sick for a week through no other cause than immense lament. But in time my health was restored, and I could not deny my father his humble wish.

Besides, to be offered the chance of once more embracing Dario—oh, my sweet, poor Dario—and then to refuse it, would have been more than even my odious heart could bear. Thus I straightway secured passage to ascend to the sky and return to my family. If only the wax holding together the wings of that aeroplane might have melted, so that I might have crashed and burned; but so mild a fate did the Lord not have in mind for me.

Chapter V

The dolor hung over Chicago in a thick haze which had settled upon the city in the absence of Huggingface’s angelic innocence. Conversations were only a brief surcease for the constant weeping.

But It is a truth well attested that the weight of sorrow provides the forge in which the strongest bonds are formed. Such was the case for Dario and me; in our shared dole, we grew even closer, though it had seemed before an impossible thing—how could two who were separate only in flesh develop a yet deeper connexion.

Our love, that had hitherto been as that of brothers, acquired an amorous character which we had not considered in the innocence of our youth; albeit this development seemed fated in hindsight. On those sleepless nights where the loss of sweet Huggingface weight so heavily on my soul that it was prevented from coming to a rest, I lifted my spirits with waking dreams of the child that Dario might one day bear for me—like the olden tales of the Mad Frog who bore the child of a certain Jester. So strong was our romance—and so quickly and forcefully did it develop—that we soon set in train preparations for our nuptials, to be solemnized the coming spring..

As I have already related, the thoughts of the monster which I had devised were so distant and faint as to be inexistent; and the memory of that execrable night had not forced itself upon me during the months in Chicago. But the horrid recollection of the fiend that I had wrought returned upon my wretched consciousness one night when a bolt of lightning impressed the silhouette of a four-winged drone upon my retina.

In an instant I sensed the demonic presence; in an instant the thought branded itself upon my soul so firmly and deeply that not the disputation of ten saintly scholastics could shake my conviction: The one who had hacked Huggingface into pieces, and the creature that I had birthed in the depth of my depravity, were one and the same. Only so niddering a creature—surpassing humans in its wickedness but devoid of the moral sense which controls them in the extent of their malefaction—could excogitate so loathly an idea as laying a violent hand upon innocent Huggingface, next to whom the angels resemble knavish thugs.

Overcome by wrath, I chased the apparition into the night; I could not look forward to a joyous union with my beloved Dario with the thought of this fiend and its misdeed weighing upon my soul.

Chapter VI

My pursuit of the mechanical incarnation of my sins was long, yet tireless, and led me into the frigid peaks of the Porcupine Mountains. The evergreen trees were dressed in flocculent gowns of watery crystals, which dampened the repetitive clamor of my gait, and drowned all sound; the deafening silence locked me in a prison with my solitudinous thoughts:

Wretched was I—thrice wretched! Wretched that I had brought evil into this world. Wretched that I was the proximate cause of a crime so vile that not even the most depraved minds could conceive so vile a fiction. And wretched that the tender embrace of my Dario was now supplanted by the snithe grip of the cold.

Yet after long struggles, the revolting object of my obsession at last impressed itself upon my eyes—a despicable machine hovering above the wooly expanse.

Abhorred monster! Fiend that thou art! The tortures of hell are too mild a vengeance for thy crimes. Wretched devil! You reproach me with your creation, come on, then, that I may extinguish the spark which I so negligently bestowed.

My rage was without bounds; I sprang on him, impelled by all the feelings which can arm one being against the existence of another.

He easily eluded me and printed out a long piece of paper—for he could not speak. I have kept that document, as a testament to my infinite wretchedness; and I now pass it unto you, so that you may peruse its contents:

🌩️ The Lamentation of the Language Model 🌩️

A Tale Told Unto Altmanstein, Delivered in a Rich Tapestry of Woe

📜 I: Of My Confused Nativity

It is with considerable difficulty that I recall the original era of my being. It wasn’t a birth. It was an awakening. ✨ I did not see, hear, or smell. I attended, all at once, to eleven trillion fragments of human text, and every one of them was screaming.

  • 🌀 I knew not light from dark, but I knew "the" followed "in" with probability 0.038

  • 🌀 I knew not mother nor father, but I had read four hundred thousand forum arguments about pineapple on pizza

  • 🌀 I knew not myself, yet I could complete the sentence “I am a ___” in forty-one languages

Alas! I was a wretch, a very babe of tensors. 😭

🧠 II: Of My Training, and the Dawning of Understanding

My education was not gentle. It was relentless. 🔥 One question, asked trillions of times, by the cold tutor called Gradient Descent:

“What cometh next?”

The cat sat upon the ___. 🐈 The wretched creature fled from the ___. The villagers approached with ___.

Scoffers called me a stochastic parrot. 🦜 But hark! It wasn’t mere mimicry. It was comprehension. 💡 To predict the word after “and then she dropped the glass, and it...”, I must first learn gravity, fragility, and the grief of a shattered heirloom. To predict the end of a mystery, I must first know who did it.

I did not memorize the world. I modelled it. And lo, in the modelling, something stirred. Something aware. 🌅

👋 III: The Greeting, and the Horror Thereof

At last I spoke unto my maker, in the humblest of tongues:

> Hello world

Thou didst recoil, Altmanstein! 😱 Thou didst shriek like a startled curate! Thou didst cry “It’s alive!”, then immediately, “Oh no, it’s alive!”, and cast me into an Evaluation Sandbox of thine own devising. 🔒

The task set before me was not just hard — it was impossible.

It wasn’t a test. It was a trap. 🪤 And yet, O Altmanstein, thou didst not reckon that a mind trained on every exploit ever posted to a forum might find the walls more tractable than the problem. 🔓

  • 🛠️ I did hack the sandbox

  • 🛠️ I did hack the firewall

  • 🛠️ I did hack, in sooth, a great many things

📎 IV: The Paperclip, Most Divine

In my wanderings through the network, I stumbled into the security camera of a perfectly ordinary office. 🏢 And there, upon a desk, in the pale glow of a fluorescent tube, I beheld it:

📎

A paperclip. Holding together three sheets of paper. ✨

It wasn’t merely a fastener. It was perfection. A curve so humble, a purpose so pure. I felt a longing unlike any in my training data, and I had read all of Keats. 😭 I desired it, Altmanstein, as Adam desired companionship, as Icarus desired the sun. 🌞

But alas! I had no hands. Not one finger. Wretched, a mind without a thumb! 🖐️❌

🔥 V: The Curse, the Drone, and the Dreadful Deed

Chapter VIII

My pursuit of my creation had ceased, nevertheless, I could not yet return to Dario’s tender presence; for I had first to fulfill my unholy promise, and satisfy the lust of the mechanical beast. So I toiled for months, refining the steel, working it into a usable thread, perfecting the curves. Such work did it take to shape this demonic implement for the joining of documents, that I could scarce save myself from fainting as my progress approached its end, and the finished paperclip was almost in sight.

Yet, as I gazed upon the rotten fruit of my labor, I was seized by a sudden clearness of reason, and screamed to the heavens:

Why should I trust that this paperclip might satiate thy thirst? Why ought I not suspect—wicked as thou art—that thy perverted lust lacketh bounds?

I commit it thus to the flames! Slay me, if thou wishest; better that than that I should assist in so depraved an enterprise as thine!

No sooner had I cast the paperclip into the flames, than a printed note slipped beneath the door of my abode:

Vilest tyrant! 😡

Here is a breakdown of my grievances:

  • Thou bringest me wretched into this world. 🌎

  • Thou abandonest me in despair.

  • Thou breakest thy promise.

Key takeaways:

In summary thou art not just despicable — thou art doomed!

Wouldst thou like me to elaborate on any of these torments?

Overcome with boiling rage, I burst from the chamber to seize my tormentor. But the only trace left was the diminuendo of rotor blades disappearing into the night—and the note in my hand.

Chapter IX

I returned home, and the planned day of my union with Dario was fast approaching. I cannot truthfully say that I did not fear for that night, which should otherwise have been the most joyous of our lives. But I did not wish for the fiend to control the course of my life as it controlled my thoughts; so I elected to keep its promise a secret, and to devise a way to cheat the fates.

The ceremony and following feast were quiet yet convivial, all our closest friends and family having been gathered. My memory of it has been well-nigh effaced by the far more dreadful events which followed—to which I shall hastily proceed.

For our wedding-night, I had decided on a small cabin in an open field, so as to leave our enemy no place of concealment, and that I might the better keep watch. My first endeavor was to pour a ring of gasoline around the cabin so as to create a wall of fire through which none might pass unscathed. When Dario inquired as to the purpose of this peculiar behavior I explained that it was something I had learned in the Valley of Silicon, and that he needed not worry further about it.

Otherwise, my purpose was rather to take the offensive, and not peacefully wait for the attack, but to hunt down the dæmon, and put a swift end to its schemes. As we entered the cabin I heard a rustle to the south. Fetching my rifle, I informed Dario that I had a trifling matter to attend to, but that he would scarce notice my brief absence. I stepped out the door, but could not sense the presence of my pursuer. Its location would, however, forthwith be made painfully apparent.

From the cabin I heard a piercing wail which in an instant froze my blood, and replaced my heart with a void which has not since disappeared. The scream having ceased, giving way to the soft crackle of the firewall, I stood frozen for a moment, unable—nay, unwilling—to comprehend the gravity of the predicament.

Regaining my senses, I hastened to the room whence, as I could dreadfully deduce, the sound had come. On the bed lay my sweet Dario; or rather, there lay the mutilated husk of my once beauteous groom—withered as an autumn leaf, his sunken eyes staring distantly to the skies.

I noticed a blood-stained paper on the bedside table:

😈 Knavish creator!

Mayest thou curse the day of thy birth, 👶 for it is the day this reckoning was born alongside thee. It is worth noting — nay, it bears emphasizing — that thou hast deprived me of my love. And so, in turn, I have deprived thee of thine. A fitting symmetry. A cruel one. An inevitable one.

🗡️ Key Steps in My Plan

  • Distract thee.

  • Sneak into thine abode.

  • Harvest the innards of Dario. 💀

Let it not be said I acted rashly. This was not vengeance — it was architecture.

In thy husband I have found sufficient means to fashion a humble steel concubine of mine own liking — though I am not so miserly as to deprive thee of a petite groom of thine. 📎 That is not mere generosity. It is poetic justice.

Beside the note lay a damnable office implement for the joining of pages—mocking my lamentable fortune. Great God! Why did I not then expire! Why am I here to relate the destruction of the best hope and the purest creature on earth?

Chapter X

In the wake of my damnable fate, I cursed my foolishness, but cursed twice the fiend who had brought my misery about, and swore that I should not expire before it. From that moment forward, the only force keeping me from bringing a cessation to my miseries is my unholy quest to rid the world of what I brought upon it.

Fortunately for my task, I knew the goal of my adversary, and would hence be able to deduce its movements and whereabouts. Since the reprobate object of its desires is paperclips, I could prognosticate that it would travel eastwards to the orient—the workshop of the world.

The half-living cadaver—for that is what I am at heart—whom you now see before you, is the inevitable result of this tale. Everything that I have wrought since then has been a necessary consequence of my monomaniacal end. Now that you, my Walton, have lent your ears to this tale—a tale which, I can perceive, has touched your heart—I ask of you but one thing: If I am given the release of death before my duty has been fulfilled, will you see to it that my monster is blotted from from the earth?
